utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters. Good morning to the Prosecution. I think there are many people who would be back home, but Happy Thanksgiving. Good morning to the Defence counsel and General Krstic. We're going to take up the testimony of yesterday's witness, but I think that we ought to have the blinds lowered before we have the witness brought into court. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues of the Prosecution and everybody else in the courtroom. Mr. President, the Defence would, at the outset of the testimony of this protected witness, like to -- that is to say, we have a series of documents, so may we go into private session straight away, which will last between five and ten minutes, because we have a series of documents to present to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, can you explain to the Trial Chamber the use of the engineers, that is to say, how can you use the engineers in the sense of control and command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The utilisation of the engineers in the sense of control and command, according to the laws and regulations that were in force in the former Yugoslav People's Army which were, in principle, translated and respected by the army of Republika Srpska - they were put into practice there, that is - the subject matter is specific, and it takes three forms or there are three possibilities for that utilisation. The first variant is the line of control and command, chain of control and command, in which the superior, the commanding officer, is in direct command of the subordinate Engineers Unit. The second possibility is the establishment of provisional groups, and the third possibility are reinforcements for subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber more detailed information with respect to the functioning of the chain of command in each of these three instances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first variant implies that control and command stems from the superior command in the sense of planning, organisation, and so forth down the line, and it gets down the line on the basis of an order issued by the authorised individual. In this case, it was the commander of the Drina Corps and the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. In a case of that kind, the individual who commands a battalion is the commander of a battalion, or his deputy, in case of the absence of the commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we come to the second variant, which is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the formation of provisional units or groups, and this is one of the most frequent ways in which the engineers are used. When the Engineers Unit of a corps goes to the formation of provisional groups, and in keeping with the tasks and assignments they are given, they function independently and autonomously and are subordinated to the individual who formed the temporary unit or the individual who authorised the person to form the provisional group, to command that provisional group or unit. These provisional groups were called groups for defensive engineering work, mobile groups for defensive engineering work, groups for the maintenance of roads, units for organising the opening of passageway and the control service and -- service of minefields, through minefields, and the Engineers Reserve Group. Therefore, the command of the Engineers Battalion in the sense of control and command with provisional formations only has responsibility to form that formation, to set it up, establish it, and to hand it over to the combat assignment where that unit is to function. He has no further command competencies over that formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, I see that in the transcript we are not differentiating between question and answer for the first variant, so I should like to ask you to tell us again, answer the following question again: What is the use of the engineers via direct orders? And please make pauses between question and answer because otherwise the court reporters are not able to follow this in the transcript. So my question is the use of engineers in the sense of control and command, that is to say, the functioning of the chain of command through direct orders. What you have already said, just repeat it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am trying to make a pause now. Perhaps I have been speaking too quickly. Let me repeat, therefore, that first part. It is the control and command directly in the chain of control and command, and it consists of the following, that the superior command sees to the planning and use of the subordinated Engineers Unit, and from that -- this means issuing orders to that subordinated unit, and those orders in a concrete case were issued by the commander and Chief of Staff. They were the two individuals who were able to issue those orders of the Drina Corps. When I say Chief of Staff, let me mention in saying so that I explained yesterday that the Chief of Staff was not automatically authorised to command, but he was ordered by the commander of the Drina Corps to perform the duties of command. So he is not automatically the person who is in command and issues commands but must be authorised to do so, and I explained this yesterday. In the chain of command, the order in the battalion is received by the commander of the battalion or his deputy in the case of his absence, if the commander is absent. He then commands further on down the line with his subordinated units. So the chain has been established from top to bottom, passing via the Engineers Unit in the sense of control and command. There is nobody from outside and no other influences or decisions can influence that chain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, this brings me to the last -- Witness DE -- Witness DE, this brings us to the last -- I apologise,; we are switched on. Witness DE, this brings us to the final and third variant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third way of command is that the superior command brings in the decision that a certain portion of manpower or materiel and technical equipment is attached to some subordinated unit, that is to say, one of the brigades. It is attached to one of the brigades. The essence of that is that, from that time on, the attached portion becomes a component part of the unit to which it is assigned and has all the -- and all the responsibilities of control and command are within the unit. That means that the battalion has nothing to do with it anymore once it has been attached, once the unit has left and been attached to this other formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, what are the competencies and authorisations of the Engineers Battalion with respect to the engineers in the brigades; that is, the corps engineers and the brigade engineers, what is the relationship between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The essence of engineers security, doesn't matter which level of command, is that it is independent and autonomous. That is how it functions. I spent a month and a half in Germany, doing some training on an exchange programme, and I was able to see that the way in which this is done in the West is different, so this is a vital question for us not to draw the wrong conclusions. In the West, the West has a direct line, the engineers line, from top to bottom. However, in our country, which is the Eastern variant, that is not the case. Each level of engineers support is completely independent. Now, what does that mean? It means that the brigade commander has his own zone of responsibility. He has his Engineers Unit which provides that security, and everything within that zone and done in that zone is, for the most part, subordinated to him. The Engineer Unit of the corps is intended to ensure units of the Drina Corps, security and support for the Drina Corps units in this case. And let us see what it in fact does. It provides support to the units who do not have their own Engineers Unit; not brigades but, for example, the artillery, for artillery positions and so on. They are the rear units. And then we have the command posts, forward command posts of the corps, and so on. If, in a certain axis, some of the provisional groups are active, the ones I mentioned a moment ago, and if they enter the zone of one of the brigades, which is rare -- that happens rarely -- but if the situation is such that it is ordered to enter the zone of the brigade, then we draw this into our plans and diagrams so that the brigade commander is aware of the fact that we have entered his zone. We colour this area in a certain way to let the commander know that we are in the zone, in his area of responsibility, doing our work there. So those two types of engineers formations have no link, no connection between the two. And perhaps military experts analysing our work in the Engineers Unit of the Drina Corps to mine and demine the terrain, they might have gained the wrong impression for a time, because (redacted), I had all the heads of brigades -- chiefs of brigades directly on the line, and that is not usual. I was in contact with them all the time. And that was because the commander of the Drina Corps had written -- had issued a written order where he ordered that method of work to be applied. So that the many documents that were to have been compiled and drafted, which the corps did not have, should be compiled for purposes of the international forces that were expected to arrive in the area. So that the picture one could have gained in the sense that the Chief of the Engineers had the chiefs of the subordinated engineers groups around him could have been erroneously seen, but we would have had to have written orders; otherwise there are no points of similarity at all between the two groups of engineers. In terms of usage, of course they were in contact when it came to information and exchanging all necessary data and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last answer in connection with the role of the Chief of Engineers refers to the period after the signing of the Dayton Accords; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It refers to the period of time, which I indicated on the document a moment ago, when I took over the duty of the Chief of Engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, I should like to know where, on what kinds of assignments portions of the unit which was under your command in June of 1995 was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should also like the usher to prepare a number of exhibits: D137, D138, D139, and D40 [as interpreted], please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about the fact that we were able to form some smaller nucleus. I didn't discuss it in detail, but I will tell you for each and every one of such corps, nucleus is what its strength was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise. Could you please enumerate the locations, first of all, and later on, in closed session, we will speak about each of them in turn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So locations where the Engineers Unit was engaged. First of all, Vis. So you don't want me to talk about the units, just about the locations; is that what you want? So Vis, the Vlasenica Brigade, Konjevic Polje Engineers Reserve Force, including the part that I spoke about yesterday. On the Drina River, there were three barge crossings: Fakovici, Osmaci, and Petrica. The construction unit was involved in the construction of the Bisina barracks and the Fakovici farm, also on the installations in Crna Rijeka, and they were working on the relay in Vlasenica. As regards the construction of the road Sase Mine-Pribicevac, they were also there, and in Konjevic Polje as well. I will talk about it later on, but I think I already mentioned it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wait for the usher to return, please. Mr. President, I think it would be advisable at this point to move into private session, and my estimate is that it would take about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you ask for a closed session or a private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, would it be possible for you to organise your examination-in-chief in such a way that we first have a public session and then one private session, so as not to go back and forth all the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I try to work in several blocks, so to speak. I think we will have one more in private session, but it was not possible for me to organise myself in a different -- in another way because of the chronology of the events that this witness is recounting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We will move into private session for several minutes and then we will go back into public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, let us go back to the issue of Drina Corps positions that were held in the area of Vis and to the work that was performed by a unit in that particular area. How many people were involved once again; for how long did they work, how long did the work last; was the work completed, and if not, when it was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already stated, a Sappers Company was involved in that work, together with their commander, who was the company commander without the group which was part of the Engineers Force Reserves which remained at Konjevic Polje. I said that there were only two or three individuals there who were providing technical support in the area the Vlasenica Brigade, and my deputy was there as well. A KN excavator was being used, one that had been at the Bisina barracks before. The excavator was used for the construction of a shelter, a company shelter on the Vis feature. And if we have a closer look at this particular portion of the text here, you will see that a bulldozer from the Zvornik Brigade was also engaged. That equipment was attached to me by the commander. You will see later on in the text that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this unit [as interpreted] was to be placed under my command. So this bulldozer was under my command. We had about ten workers from the Engineers Company who were involved in the repairing of roofs and in an attempt to salvage the houses that had been set on fire. Practically the whole area was destroyed, and the brigade commander, who happened to be from that particular village, found himself in front of his burnt-down house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, in the record we see that a unit was placed under your command. Is that correct? Or was it only a piece of technical equipment that was placed under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was only this piece of technical equipment, that is, the bulldozer, that was placed under my command, and not any unit. The vehicle was placed under the command of the battalion, the Osmaci Battalion, and didn't have any direct connection with the Zvornik Brigade, but it was placed under my command for the purpose of this particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The essence of our assignment was the following: Mine and explosive obstacles that had been destroyed previously had to be placed there once again. The commander probably thought that another more fierce attack can be expected, and that is why we were engaged in putting up these more enforced obstacles, reinforced obstacles. So a shelter was being constructed, the Vis shelter, because of the very high number of casualties that the unit had sustained earlier on and we realised that the shelter was not very good because we always had many casualties there, many wounded soldiers, and so on. The biggest problem regarding the Vis feature was actually the fact that it was very deep towards the Muslim-held territory and its flanks were exposed. There was only one road, one route that led to the Vis feature, and it went along the Brenan Ridge [phoen]. But no vehicle could negotiate that route; only individuals. So whenever we had casualties, it was very difficult for us to carry out an evacuation. The Chief of Staff of the corps, the Chief of Staff, that is, ordered me to try and solve the problem of that axis, of that route, and I thought about it and I thought that the best idea was to dig it in so that we can have a vehicle move along that road, along that trench, so to speak, without being exposed to enemy fire. So that was the kind of construction work that we had to work on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long did the work take and how many people did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I told you about the people who worked. I said that we had about ten people working on the repair work, on the houses. We had about 15 Sappers in total, together with the commander. We also had two Cobras and two other construction vehicles -- one was mine, one was from the Zvornik Brigade -- and we had people who serviced those vehicles. Of course, I used the assistance of the battalion itself in the sense that they provided some kind of technical support on a regular basis, and it was the battalion that needed our construction services, so they assisted us as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that we remained there until the end of the war. The Vis feature was very important for us in terms of engineers support, and certain portions of my unit were still there at the end of the work and they were engaged in all kinds of construction and repair work. I don't know whether you want to know where I personally was, but troops stayed in the area all the time. Later on, there were NATO airstrikes and they targeted the Vis feature. And then after those airstrikes, of course, we had to carry out additional construction work, so remained there for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: D139, this document pertains to the demining work in the area of responsibility of the battalion. When did you receive this particular order and how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the details regarding this particular order, because I was at the Vis feature at the time. However, the person who signed the order as a duty officer briefed me a day later or so about the order when we spoke on the telephone. And one can see from the document that seven Sappers were involved there, together with the company commander. This relates to the engineers communications work, and this type of work was described in the instruction, in the relevant instruction, which provided as follows: If the use of that unit should be ordered by the commander, he is -- he was supposed to carry out that particular work. So everything was regulated in that particular instruction. So it was obvious that the Corps Commander, at that point in time, in terms of using the engineers force, was in a very critical situation. He had already used everything he had, and at that particular moment he made a sudden decision to use this reserve formation, that is, the Sappers Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, I don't think it is necessary to discuss every particular location where your unit was engaged in detail, but I should like to know the following: All these locations that you have spoken about, aside from the area of Zeleni Jadar and the demining work of the Sappers Unit, which was described in document D539 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We haven't heard the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- all the work that was carried out by your force there was of a defensive character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was all defensive work. And the area in question was the area towards Tuzla. We had to protect ourselves from the actions of the Tuzla Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only on the 5th of July, which is when Defence Exhibit 139 relates to, you were in a position for the first time to deploy your unit and use it in an action of an attack character; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, how many people, bearing in mind that your unit was scattered around the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, it had been dispersed, how many people at the beginning of July, or, more exactly, after the 5th of July, were in Konjevic Polje? How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje at that time, that is to say, from my departure, there were about ten people, minus one commanding officer with a rank. That is to say, we had the following parts of the unit: We had the logistics platoon and we had my part of the -- which -- we referred to it as "the command," but they were ordinary soldiers, privates, without any rank, and we had the communications department. The communications department had two men manning it. Of those two, one at that time was at Vis and the other one stayed on. Of the command there were three people there, and the rest was the logistics platoon. Due to the extremely critical situation with regard to providing security and support for Konjevic Polje, I had -- I devised a solution, which I don't know whether it was used in the Army of Republika Srpska at all before that. I was not able to solve the problem of providing security for the warehouses in Konjevic Polje. And then in the municipality of Milici, I went there and asked the organs of civilian authority to find six men who would be -- serve as guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- I understand that narratives are appropriate in some context here, however, this is not a lay witness and the question was asked not about security in Milici. I would request that we try to go as question/answer as best we can. I sympathise with Mr. Visnjic's problems here, but I think this is taking a lot of time and we're going off into areas that I don't find relevant, and we're not going in a question and answer. We're getting very long narratives. That would be my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Visnjic, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the witness wished to explain how his manpower was increased, and I don't see that that has anything to do with the security of Milici. I'll check it in the transcript. But as I heard the witness' answer, he was answering the question that was asked him, and that was with respect to how many men his unit had. I shall try to guide the witness and make him as brief as possible, but we're getting into a critical point now and I think that it is necessary for the witness to speak in detail about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps we ought to go to the core of the matter, the heart of the matter, as quickly as possible. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to prepare Exhibit 160/A and 160/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, perhaps we could go on for five minutes and then take a break. Five more minutes, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, while we're waiting for the exhibits, could you tell the Trial Chamber, please: In Konjevic Polje, you were there until the 9th of July, when you went on leave for private reasons, and you returned there at around the 20th of July; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to leading. If we are in the core of the matter, I would prefer to hear the answers from the witnesses and not have them suggested by the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you have heard the objection raised. Please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, until when were you in the Konjevic Polje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago through this order, that is to say, I showed when I left Konjevic Polje. It was when the engagement at Vis started. As for the area of the Drina Corps, I left that area on the 9th, and I returned to the Drina Corps area on the 20th. I left the area from -- I left Vis, that is to say, I went to the command, Corps Command, Corps headquarters. I think that was in the evening hours. Whether it was on the 8th or 9th, I'm not quite sure, but it was in the evening of that day, and from the Corps Commander I was given permission to leave to see my family. I returned on the 20th. I went to Vis, and seeing certain changes with respect to my unit's engaged, I arrived at Konjevic Polje. I was in Konjevic Polje for perhaps two days, and then returned again to Vis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you told us the days but didn't tell us the month or the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was July, from the 9th to the 20th, of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Prosecution Exhibit 160/A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a map of Konjevic Polje and the broader area around it incorporated by the Bratunac-Kravica-Konjevic Polje roads and the Zvornik-Vlasenica road. Your unit was located near the junction at Konjevic Polje; is that correct --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say something at this point. There is something that hasn't been probably understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, may I interrupt? I think that now we have reached the heart of the matter, so please make sure not to make leading questions. Your question should be, "Where was your unit?" You can't speak instead of the witness, so no leading questions. We're at the heart of the matter now, and please pay attention not to ask leading questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, could you explain this to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up till now, I have been talking about where my unit was. Konjevic Polje is one of the locations where part of my unit was located. So the command post was at Vis, but part of the unit, as I described it earlier on, was locate -- was in that locality. I did not count all the localities that I was engaged in, but one of the localities was Konjevic Polje. I see that conclusions have been drawn frequently in the sense that this was the locality of my unit and that this was its permanent position, permanent post. My military post, when I was set up as a unit and all the elements of development of my unit, were Milici, and I gave to the Prosecution a document with the military post and its number, which I have now forgotten; but it was Milici, and Milici was the collection area, and within the context of its assignments, it found itself located in Konjevic Polje at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is an ideal moment for a break, and we're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, did you, at your post in 1995, did you take any work in the planning of engineering security for the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, were you acquainted with the plan of operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, do you know how many of your men and in which way took part in the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krivaja 95? Are you thinking of the operation around the Srebrenica enclave; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the attack and assuming control of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see the document, and from what I have stated so far, it is obvious that in the attack on the enclave of my parts, the Sapper department took part which entered within the composition of the Skelani portion, and we can see that from the document, that is to say, to open passage for the defence of the Skelani feature. I never linked the two together, but they can be placed into a context. That is to say, the road that was constructed up there, we -- the work took a month and a half; we started before these events. The road was used in the context of the operation, but it was not built for that purpose. And the main financier of that road and most of the composition up there was from the Bratunac municipality whose interest it was to have the Serbian population return to the Serbian villages that had been left empty. Later on, when I returned -- but the operation had already been concluded -- I came upon two of my compositions in combat activity already turned towards Zepa, which is not that, so I don't know whether you need to know that. It was the Sapper. A Sapper Company from these was transferred to the Zepa area of combat, and the loaders were with that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that loader, where was it engaged before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was engaged at Pribicevac within the group working on the road construction. And during that operation, it was engaged probably, I did not issue any more assignments because this TG, tactical group, Pribicevac in its position, it's difficult to speak about that because it existed at one point and not at another. But the command cadre in the TG Pribicevac was the responsible authority for engaging that part of the unit, so when the attack started, the loader was used to follow the movement of units moving from Pribicevac to the road going towards Jadar. I think that was the road they used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would be the southern side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the only road, although I'm not well acquainted with the infrastructure there, but the only road that the loader could move along was the road towards Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher now to show the witness Exhibit 160/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you have before you a satellite image of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a picture taken on the 27th of July, 1995, and we will be using it for the purpose of explaining to the Trial Chamber how the soldiers were deployed and positioned from your unit at the beginning of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is rather a narrow image and it is difficult to focus on the whole area of my unit. For me to be able to explain this, let me explain why I came to Konjevic Polje. I explained all the other localities, but not the locality of Konjevic Polje. I came to Konjevic Polje pursuant to an order of the command of the Drina Corps to do repair work on the terrain -- the facilities, the buildings, and so on -- so that the refugees from Central Bosnia could take up residence there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little, please, speak a little more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, so that the refugees from Central Bosnia, the Nisic Plateau, and Sarajevo could have somewhere to live, and there were a lot of refugees for whom we did not have accommodation. We had no solution for them in the Drina Corps. So I started on my repair work, and I started the settling of the area. Had this picture been taken much earlier on, my unit would be in quite a different part of Konjevic Polje. This is the final phase of the operation. I didn't move from this locality afterwards. But the initial stage in Konjevic Polje was quite -- in quite another part, towards Zvornik, and I did repair work on the houses and buildings, and the population was able to receive accommodation there. So my locality moved and changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to go back to my question: On Exhibit 160/1, indicate for us, please, where the soldiers of your unit were located at the beginning of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of July 1995, the exact location -- I'm going to speak about two types of location: locations that were manned at the time of these events, that is to say, from about the 10th to the 20th, for example; and facilities that were used when the unit came to Konjevic Polje. This facility here, it was a small one and it was the communications department. This building next door was the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For purposes of the record, the witness is indicating to the group of buildings in the left-hand corner of Exhibit 160/1, far left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two buildings here in the "A" square were not actually used with respect to the unit's location, but we used them as a technical warehouse. We had reserve -- spare parts there. And when they were in Konjevic Polje, two mechanics worked there repairing the spare parts from the logistics platoon, but nobody was put up there. Around these buildings, we had this area here. They were not used at all; they were just to mask -- used as masks, and I'll explain what I mean by their masking purpose. For operational purposes. Opposite, there was a plateau, and I can't quite distinguish it here. There was a trailer for the transport of engineering material, but it was out of order. It didn't have any wheels and we were not able to replace the wheels, and therefore it was never used. I took it from the SP centre in Bijeljina, and I wanted to make a plateau trailer out of it, a functional plateau trailer. However -- a flat-bed trailer. But it was out of order. Perhaps there was something else parked there, but it was not of any importance to me. This central feature that we see here, central building, was the school. When I started working at Konjevic Polje, the school was already refurbished as a military facility, but with the intention of putting up the manoeuvring brigade of the Drina Corps in the school building, which was to be formed at that time. However, the brigade was not established at that time. It was never formed then. So we turned the interior in the quartermaster residence [as interpreted], that is to say, for units who were passing by and for the MUP forces. And I'm speaking about the time period that I was there. Different units passed through and were accommodated there. I myself used an adjacent building --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, never mind the details now. We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buildings in this upper corner consist of three buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is in the "B" square, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite see, but in this square, in these three houses, we put up the Engineers Company, the Road and Bridge Company, and the Logistics Platoon. The Engineers Company, after repairing the buildings and facilities in Konjevic Polje, never actually had need to come here. But from time to time perhaps somebody did come for some repair work or to do minor repairs in Konjevic Polje, so that this building was kept locked for the most part of the time. The building next to it was a building where we put up the Road and Bridge Company. When I say "company," a company is equal to 10 men. Before that, I only had the cores of these -- nucleus of these groups. So this was the Road and Bridge Company, and the building down below was the building where we accommodated the Logistics Platoon. The building in the corner here is the quartermaster warehouse, which is where we kept our food and everything else needed for the work of the kitchens. And women slept there, the women working as cooks in the kitchens. Over here, and you can't see it on the map, actually quite a long way away, about 300 metres, there was another building in which I had my mines and explosives stored. So along the road here towards Bratunac, that's where it was. It was a sort of a warehouse for mines and explosives. Opposite here, in these buildings, I had a few livestock, some animals that we fed and kept for our -- for nutrition and so on. So that would be that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just go back a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask the questions please, Witness DE. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, please, where the guard posts were at the beginning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a plan and project for the security of Konjevic Polje, and there were six guard posts, according to that plan; however, that maximum level of security was to be used when the units were there and when we were able to man all those points, if the units were there, as I say. When the units were not there, when they were all on assignment and when we were not able to ensure this kind of security, I only had three guard posts. The first guard post was geared toward securing this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. For purposes of the record, it is the rectangular shape in the upper right-hand corner of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Over here was the kitchen attached to the school, adjoining the school on the right-hand side. This was guard post number one. Guard post number two was located by the command facility and the communications centre, which is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For purposes of the record once again, the witness is indicating the area in the bottom right-hand corner of Exhibit 160/1 -- to the left, not the bottom right-hand corner, left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over here, in this part which can't be seen on the photograph. It is fairly high up. I wanted to gain in height, so we went up to the position here. If the unit was there, that's where the post would have been. There's a Muslim cemetery up here, and it was a little below this cemetery that we set up guard post three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, for purposes of the record, guard post number three was outside the photograph, in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guard post number four was approximately in this region here, a little above this. Somewhere there. Perhaps a little higher. It's difficult to locate the exact spot now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, for purposes of the record, guard post number four was located near the title where it says "Facility Housing Drina Corps, 5th Engineering Battalion," a little above that title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guard post number five cannot be seen on this image, but it would be somewhere in this corner up here. A little further up. About 200 metres further up, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, for purposes of the record, guard post five is outside the photograph, in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guard post six is along this road here, about 150 metres ahead, on this side of the road. Opposite that guard post was the warehouse for the explosives and mines, and that guard post was designed to provide security for the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For purposes of the record once again, guard post number six, not included on the photograph, but it is along the road on the right-hand side of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The security regime at that time, as the units were all on assignment, was as follows: Guard post number one was security for the Logistics Platoon and up to -- manned by the -- guard post number two, we called it a guard post, but it was the duty officer, the signalsman, the man from communications, someone from the command as well, they all manned this guard post; but during the day, actually, the guard post did not exist. The duty officer worked inside during the day and stood guard at night. Guard post number six, which I said cannot be seen on this photograph, was manned by the soldiers, although I don't know if I can refer to them as soldiers. We called them "guards." We referred to them as guards. They were sent to me from the Defence Ministry of Milici. They were assigned to me from them. They did not have -- they were either too old or they were sick or wounded, so they were not able to be proper soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness Defence Exhibit D99.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, do you know Spaso Bandjur and Vaso Orasanin? Do you know these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know them. They are the two guards in question. They used to come at 3.00 by bus to Konjevic Polje and return at 7.00. So this guard post was not manned throughout the day, but only in the night hours during the night. So the warehouse was controlled by means of a patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English version of the D99 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, are these people, the two individuals that I just mentioned, Spaso Bandjur and Vaso Orasanin, I should like to know whether they were wounded on the 13th of July as it is stated here in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was signed and composed, actually, by my deputy. What you said in relation to this document is quite correct. I can only give you my comment, but I wasn't personally there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had returned from your leave, what were you briefed about by your deputy? You said that you came back on the 20th or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't have any special briefing, but as I would encounter my assistants, they would provide me with the relevant information. As regards this particular document, my assistant for logistics told me about this document because I happened to see him, because the deputy was at Han Pogled where the TV relay was at the time. I have to say that the signal that was coming from us -- to us from Yugoslavia was turned off, so the relay had to be turned towards Bijeljina. That was his main task; that is why he went there, so I didn't find him when I came back. At any rate, the information that I received was that on the 13th of July, in the early morning hours, an attack occurred against the guard post number six. Out of three guards who were present there at the time, two were wounded. I didn't tell you anything about the kind of defence that I had in mind for Konjevic Polje and what I did to that effect. I must say that, as an engineers officer without enough troops, I tried to use my resources as much as it was possible. The area that I just indicated was very well mined and closed on the flanks, and it could be entered only from two directions, from two axes: from the Bratunac, along the road, and also from the village of Konjevic Polje itself, which was on the other side. So what happened here was the following: The unit that carried out the attack started advancing towards Konjevic Polje. I don't know what exactly they had in mind, what kind of target, but they came to a minefield and two mines were activated, and then the shooting ensued, and in the shooting, two guards that I just mentioned were wounded. From this, you can see that individuals in question were transferred to the Zvornik Medical Centre. Why? At that point in time, practically speaking, Konjevic Polje was cut off and encircled, because the front part of the column of the 28th Division had cut off the communication with Milici, whereas the second axis on which parts of that unit were moving was at Kuslat, which was situated a little further down below Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So as regards this particular incident, I thought that whoever was leading the column along the Konjevic Polje-Milici route, having observed the situation, they must have concluded that there were not many troops in Konjevic Polje. That's the only idea I can think of, because this was actually the first encounter with the passing column. So the column was passing and nothing was happening, so I think that somebody just wanted to check out the situation, and they stepped on a mine, shooting occurred, and two individuals were wounded. I don't know what happened later on because we were separated. There was this minefield between us. So because of the passage of the column towards Milici, the wounded individuals were not transferred to Milici, which was our field hospital for our troops, but were transported to Zvornik, and it was only possible to do that after parts of the police force had arrived from the direction of Zvornik to Konjevic Polje. And when we were actually officially told that the wounded could be transported to Zvornik, only at that time were they actually transported to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have just told us is something that you were briefed about by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not official. This is what I discussed with my assistant for logistics and then later on with my deputy. I have to say that my deputy personally escorted the two wounded soldiers to Zvornik, and on his own initiative, because the communication had been cut off, he left for the Vis feature. And he asked the battalion commander, the Osmaci Battalion commander, that the Sappers Unit, that the Sapper portion of the unit, which was completing its job at Vis, be returned to Konjevic Polje because, practically speaking, he was no longer able to do his job. This guard post was out of usage. And we had to provide adequate protection and security for this mines and explosive warehouse, which was indeed very important for us, and we couldn't allow the enemy to destroy it or get hold of it. So he transmitted that request to the commander and he agreed with him that that unit should be returned, and he came back to Konjevic Polje Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sometime during the night. And the unit in question, that is, those 15 Sappers, arrived in Konjevic Polje on the following day, because it could not have been done right away, due to the combat activities. They needed some time to pull out from the area and from the work that they were performing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the usher to show the witness Exhibits 160/7, 5, 6 -- those are satellite photographs, please. 160/5, 6, and 7. 160/6, if we can have that one first, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you have a satellite photograph in front of you which was taken on the 5th of July, 1995. In relation to this -- actually, what we see is an enlarged portion which was marked as part B on the Exhibit number 160/1. On this photograph, one can see a tractor with a trailer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher Exhibit number 160/7 to be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... try to clarify it. I believe the one that had A, B, C on it, the enlargement, was 160/1, and that was 27 July. And just to clarify that. I know there was one up there that had 5 July on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is true that 160/1 is dated 27th of July. However, on the document number 160/6, which is dated the 5th of July, shows the same portion of the photograph that was taken on the 27th of July. I just want to identify the portion that was indicated as part B. I hope I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Actually, I'm not sure, but please proceed. But the photograph of the 5th of July is not an enlarged portion of the photograph of the 27th of July, of course, so we have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may have been an error in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to Exhibit 160/7, which is on the ELMO. This photograph shows a tractor with a trailer as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about this machine, please, about this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what it was called, the military farm of the Drina Corps. I don't know it, but perhaps it's not that important. Anyway, the vehicle belonged to the military farm of the Drina Corps, and it happened to be in Konjevic Polje for the purpose of some agricultural work which had taken place earlier on, and one of the tractors that was used for that purpose was this one. During this period of time, I think it was out of order, and I don't think that anyone was there servicing the vehicle because no such work was taking place at the time. So once again, this vehicle belonged to the military farm, which was involved in agricultural work in Konjevic Polje. So that work was carried out by the members of the military farm, not us. But I think that this tractor was there for the purposes of being maintained or serviced. I'm not sure. It belonged to me at the time. But I don't think that at this particular point in time, I don't think that it was in order, and the person who operated this machine was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, was this vehicle used for the transport of bodies of the BH army soldiers who had surrendered on the road at Konjevic Polje-Kravica and who were subsequently executed, as it has been testified by witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that that was the case. I had a number of soldiers there, and I must say once again that they had lots of difficulties maintaining these security -- these guard posts. This is a relatively large area, and I don't think that at any point in time any of my troops abandoned it. They were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us stay with this photograph of the 27th of July for a while. On this shot, unlike the one on the 5th of July, we can see some other vehicles in the vicinity of the buildings which were, as you said, under the control of your unit. Could you tell us anything about these vehicles and how they happened to be there on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can tell on this photograph, one can see a loader and two FAP tracks. Sometime around the 25th or 26th of July, the Sappers Unit stopped its engagement in the area of -- in the theatre of operation towards Zepa and came back. I know that the combat activities towards Zepa were taking place for a while, but as soon as the defence lines were down, the Engineers Force were no longer needed in terms of opening up the roads and providing engineers support. As regards the direction from which it came from, the bauxite mines -- I'm not familiar with the area and I don't know those many locations that were used. So from that direction, from that particular road, movements of mechanisation was not allowed during that period of time towards Zepa. It was actually not possible because only mountain units together with appropriate mechanisation was able to move along that area. So that is why that particular portion was pulled out from the combat operation zone and returned to Konjevic Polje. At that time, the duty operations officer transmitted an order to me at the Vis feature to the effect that I should assist the cleaning of the city of Srebrenica, which was undertaken by the civilian authorities there. The reason why they requested our help was the fact that there had been some unfortunate incidents in the city, in the town itself or its immediate surroundings, because of the mines. So I was required to solve a very difficult and serious problem in Srebrenica involving a small river or a creek which passes through Srebrenica. I don't remember its name. On that creek, a number of mini-transformer stations or hydroelectric plants had been set up, and those small units or energy plants were being used in Srebrenica. Such stations were makeshift stations, but I believe that they were, they were usable during that period of time. There was a kind of collector underneath this river, and my task was to solve all the construction problems relating to that. Two individuals had been killed at one of those mini-plants because of a booby trap, and this is why these two FAP tracks were returned because I wanted to use them for the transport of the debris that would be there as a result of our construction work in Srebrenica. So this action was, as I said, undertaken by civilian authorities, but this particular work involving those mini-plants was assigned to us because of the danger of booby traps and mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to put the exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 165 on the ELMO -- or 160/5, and also to have Defence Exhibits 146 and 145 prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we will be working until 10 minutes past 12, so that you can organise yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, once again I'm showing you a satellite photograph that was taken on the 27th of July, 1995. The photograph shows a number of trucks and one other Engineers Force vehicle next to them. So was this vehicle in the function of the previously-described work involving the cleaning of the town of Srebrenica, was the vehicle there for that purpose on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This vehicle was VAT 3 and it was never used during the war. I don't see any particular function, any particular task for which it could be used. That kind of a vehicle has a part that is attached to it on the side, and it makes rows. This vehicle, I don't know why it was there. I don't know how it could be used for any kind of work, for any kind of purpose. I don't know. It could only be used for making a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit number 145, 146, one after the other so that the Chamber can have a picture of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, what you can see here is an enlarged portion of the OTP Exhibit 160/9 and 8. It is a detail from a much larger photograph, the one that you have still in front of you, perhaps. Two details that were taken on different dates, on the 5th of July and the 27th of July. A vehicle can be seen in the right-hand corner on both of these photographs. Could you tell us what that could be? What is that kind of vehicle that is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. This could be -- but really, I'm not sure. This could be the TAM truck that we mentioned, the one from Zvornik, the one that I mentioned yesterday when I talked about the handover of duty. That vehicle was used for rear logistics, and -- well, if it was my vehicle, I think that that could only have been this TAM truck that I already spoke about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many loaders did you have in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the usher to show to the witness Exhibit number 160/2, and also to have Exhibits number -- OTP Exhibits 160/2, 177, and Defence Exhibit D144, to have them prepared, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise this photograph, Witness DE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the school building, the school in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put Exhibit number OTP 177 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, what is the exhibit number of this photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. It wasn't entered in the record. It is D160/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I think it should be "P" because it is a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, you're quite right. OTP 160/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to place OTP 177 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, are you familiar with this photograph and what it shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the outside booth which is part of the school building, the reception booth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, did your unit stay or was it at some point in time holding the positions that can be seen on this photograph at the beginning of July 1995 until your return from leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to comment on this photograph because I should need the whole building, the entire building in the photograph; however, let me try to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, sorry to interrupt you. Could you please just answer my question with "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, did any other unit of the Drina Corps have control of the facilities which can be seen on the photographs 160/A and 177?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the exhibit in question is Exhibit 160/2. Could I now ask the usher to show to the witness Defence Exhibit 144. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is an enlarged portion of an aerial photograph, Exhibit number OTP 160/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you wanted to tell us something more about this location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Konjevic Polje to do the construction work and the repair work there, the only facility which I did not have the right to use was the school here. Then I insisted on being given at least a portion of it, because it was necessary for me to have access to water, and I also needed a kitchen, and the school had those facilities. So they allowed me to use one part of the school building, this part here. And in this corner that you can see on the photograph, we had a certain amount of coal which was used for cooking. This was used for central heating, and we turned it into a kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness is indicating the upper right protruding wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this area here was used by the Sappers Unit when it was in the area, when it was there, and the last soldier who left the area was the one who left together with the detachment that went to Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 5th of July. We saw a document describing that a moment ago. In this part here, there used to be a WC, a toilet, but the Sapper Unit had some of its quartermaster items there and supports, although there was no control there; it was never locked. But anything they didn't need, they would place into that building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For purposes of the record, the witness has indicated the upper left-hand part of the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This part here was the school, and it had two floors, two storeys, and for the Manoeuvre Brigade, all the rooms were used as dormitories, sleeping rooms. Only in this corner here, on the ground floor, there was a room with tables and chairs in it, and it was used for meetings and as a kitchen. And I asked them to place that room at my disposal as well, for me to be able to convene a meeting or to have -- for my men to have a proper meal there, sitting down at a table, if it was raining outside. But each of these buildings had small dining rooms, makeshift dining rooms, for the men to be able to eat there. I was not permitted to do so, but I was told that I could turn it into a dining room if I could ensure that I had an entrance to it, and what I did was to knock down the wall here and make a separate entrance which was not linked up to the school proper, so I didn't have to go through the school building but was able to go through this separate side entrance if I wanted to use that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Witness DE, at the beginning of July, did your unit use those portions of the building which you have just indicated and described to us after the 5th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last soldier to leave before those events was this detachment on the 5th. I said that Simanic left on the 13th, in the evening, and that he asked the company to return, and it returned to Konjevic Polje on the 14th, at around noon. From that time on, it was in this section of the building. Those 15 or so men were there. However, as we did not complete the company's engagement, it left on the 15th and went to take up its assignment towards Zepa, because on the 15th those units entered a minefield, suffered heavy casualties, were not able to solve the situation, and went -- that is to say, there was one day when those 15 people were ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's summarise briefly. Part of the building after the 5th of July was used by your soldiers, in the period between the 14th in the afternoon until the 15th in the morning, when they left once again; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As we're talking about the departure of the Sapper Company, did they go to Zepa? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th, they left for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What axis were they active in around Zepa, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there, so I don't know specifically, but I know that they were introduced somewhere from the direction of the bauxite mine, from that area and that approach to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just slow down a little, please. Do you know what unit they worked with there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think a tactical group was formed and that they were attached to the commander of that tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that tactical group was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. As I wasn't there, I don't know, but there was a tactical group that had been established from the units that attacked from that axis. You probably know from the rest of the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know which units were within the composition of that tactical group, or one unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume -- I can only assume, because it was the Milici Brigade and parts of the Bratunac and Skelani ones. They went from that direction. That is on the basis of logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned from your leave, you found them there, together with a portion of the technical part, on the Zepa axis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My main task was Vis. I was responsible for the situation at Vis, so my task continued to be Vis, but I had to go to Konjevic Polje to size up the situation and to see what further steps I could take. I did not go to the zone where this unit was carrying out combat activities. I was only informed that it was there and of its composition. I know that the department joined it which was within the composition of the Skelani Battalion, so at that time, up there had been completed; it was complete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "up there." Where are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the axis where it was deployed. I don't know -- I can't locate it exactly because I wasn't actually there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we are talking about Zepa, are we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the axis of deployment of that tactical group, where that tactical group was attacking, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, perhaps this would be an opportune moment to take a break. But before we do so, Mr. Visnjic, let me remind you that you said that this witness would be testifying for about four hours, so please do your sums, and I think you'll realise that we're almost at the end of that time. But anyway, let us take a break of 50 minutes. We have this siren, the noise of this siren that seems to be going on and on, but I suppose it's doing what it's supposed to do. So we're going to reconvene at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we have until 3.00, so, in order to divide up our work, we're going to have a ten-minute break at around 2.00. So bearing that in mind, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I should like to inform the Trial Chamber that General Krstic is absent for health reasons, and the Defence has tabled a statement to that effect to the registrar, handed it to the registrar, and he will be absent to the end of today's proceedings. Probably after a doctor has examined him, we shall know whether he will be attending tomorrow or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Visnjic. We should like to wish the General all the best. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, we showed you a set of exhibits, Prosecution exhibits, 160/2 and 177 and Defence Exhibit 144, which is on the monitor. A protected witness, Witness S of the Prosecution, during his testimony stated that he was brought to the building, to the guard building which was identified on these photographs, and he later described the procedure, the conduct towards him, what was done with him. My question is the following: When you returned to your unit, were you informed of whether or not your soldiers took part in the capture of a certain number of soldiers or civilians belonging to the BiH army, members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the information which I received, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in the buildings that have been described that there were some other units present there. Could you please wait for me to put my question to you. Did those units belong to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left and when I returned to the building, the units weren't there; however, the school was used to accommodate some of the units, some units. Which units, I do not know because my units and those units had no connection at all with respect to assignment. We had nothing to do with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether some of those units were subordinated to your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The -- in practice in the Engineering Unit, nothing is attached. It is a unit that can be -- units can be attached to others, but nothing can be attached to this particular unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your unit subordinated to any other unit in your environment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Let me put it this way: If we're thinking about part of the unit that was in Konjevic Polje, if you're thinking about that, then the answer is no; and we said a moment ago that some units were subordinated in other localities to something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "My unit" referred to the part of the unit located in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then my answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, can you describe to the Trial Chamber the -- what kind of communications your unit used? And I'm thinking about the part of it stationed in Konjevic Polje. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to prepare OTP Exhibit 521.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit was undergoing the process of development, and it was a very modest unit in terms of facilities. And in the communications department, it had very poor facilities there, too, very bad possibilities. In Konjevic Polje at the end of a wire link which was linked to the Milici Brigade, we had a field telephone. It was a telephone that we all used. We had no other communication at all. We had, in addition to that, two other field -- in addition to that, we had two other field telephones which were linked to each other, to one another, and they -- the line was drawn from the facility I pointed out a moment ago where the logistics base was to the command. And as this is quite a distance, this saved people from going back and forth, so it ensured communication between these two points. But they were not within any other system of communications, nor could they be used apart from within that one line, from telephone to telephone. In addition to that equipment, I had a radio device. It was the RUP 12, R-U-P 12 device, and two Motorolas. Those communication facilities always attended the Sappers Unit, and the RUP 12 had as its task to ensure communication between the Sapper Unit and the command of the unit for whom we were performing the work. And the two Motorolas were used to establish communications between the group laying the minefields and another group which was providing security facing the enemy. So that's all I had with respect to communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. So when your Sapper Unit left, what remained of the communication equipment at Konjevic Polje? What do you suppose, assume [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have to suppose or assume anything. I took the RUP to Vis with me with the two Motorolas, so that in Konjevic Polje there was only this wire link with the Milici Brigade; that is to say, a wire was stretched across the road, and at the end of that wire there was a field telephone, whereas internal communications was based on two telephones not linked to any other system, and that was between the logistics department and the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your unit have a code name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit did not have a code name, a secret name, nor did I have one, but the exchange -- that is to say, the end of that line was called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Communications centre, but it was a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That last wire link, wire line, did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I would like -- the interpreters are asking if you could speak into the microphone, please. They're having trouble following.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that last wire link that you mentioned a moment ago, was its name Carina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the word, "Carina."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to place OTP Exhibit 521, the English version, on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] OTP Exhibit 521 cannot be placed on the ELMO because it is confidential, and we would have to move into private session if you wished to have it placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Yes, I know the reason for that. If my colleague Mr. McCloskey agrees, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We did see that go across, and I believe that the one you were about to put on the ELMO had the initials blotted off, which means that that was not under seal. But if you can -- which may solve things. The one you were about to put on, I believe, was the bis, that was okay, but we can take a look. We can confirm it and try to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps we could move into private session, because the next question from another area would also require a private session, and that would be the last set of questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have 521 bis, which is right there. That's not under seal and shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all events, do you still wish to move into private session, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
