utterances.text: My name is being mentioned here, so I don't want it to go out in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I would like us to move into private session, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, did the soldiers from your unit take part in the disturbance of the graves in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, together with General Krstic, you actively took part in the implementation of the Dayton Accords. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this -- what your function -- not your function. Can you explain to us what General Krstic's work comprised of? What was his role and his cooperation with international forces and also with the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's calling for a conclusion on the part of this witness that there's been no foundation laid that he knows that. General Krstic has had a chance to testify. He can talk about his own involvement, but it seems -- unless there's a foundation that there's some close working together, it puts us -- we're not able to now cross-examine an actor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, perhaps it would be -- we could put a framework to the witness' part in this along the lines of what Mr. McCloskey has just suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked -- I think I asked the witness in detail if they worked together towards implementing the Dayton Agreements, then what was his function or the function of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic, but that is a conclusion. You worked together, but what did you do; when; where did we go; meetings with certain individuals; that could set a framework to his participation, determine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that Mr. McCloskey, during the cross-examination, can try to clarify the issue. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My only issue is if he makes conclusions about what General Krstic is doing, if we can know that he is with him at the time or that -- because if he just goes into talking about General Krstic, we don't know if he heard about that from someone else or whether or not he was with him at the time. I don't have an objection to him talking about General Krstic, of course, but just going into conclusions about General Krstic without clearly establishing where he fits into it will put us in a situation, it would be very difficult to follow. And this is -- obviously, Dayton is not necessarily a big issue for us, so I don't want to make a big deal out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must admit that I'm somewhat handicapped here because the witness had spoken for more than 14 hours with the OTP, so they probably know in advance what his answers will be. I am asking rather general questions, I know, because I'm not quite sure as to what kind of details he will be talking about. Perhaps we should ask the witness this question, and let's see what he has to say. If he speaks in too great a detail, then perhaps I can interrupt him and guide him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic, proceed with your question, and then we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, did you participate together with General Krstic in the negotiations regarding the implementation of the Dayton Accords, in particular as regards the procedure of demining the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The main reason why I left my post (redacted) (redacted) was actually the implementation of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber, could you describe to the Chamber, in brief terms, the role of General Krstic in that specific area of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His role at the time as the Corps Commander was rather significant because that whole part of the work which involved the military aspect of the implementation of the Dayton Accords was the responsibility for the Corps Commander. He was the one who had to spell it out, who had to carry out the necessary preparations and organise the work. One of the very important segments of this part of the accord was the area of responsibility of the chief engineer officer. General Krstic was present there at all times, and he encouraged me in my work, and he insisted on the quality of the work that had to be performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, let us try to summarise this particular area, and let me help you with a question. Could you tell us something about General Krstic as a commanding officer, since you had an opportunity to spend quite some time with him? And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you would please let me finish this issue regarding the Dayton Agreement and his attitude towards it. I remember an incident that took place in the area of the Main Staff when the soldiers of the 2nd Armoured Unit wanted to accomplish a certain task and then something happened, there was a misunderstanding of some sort, and we had an official ban to contact the forces. The following day, I had a meeting with Colonel Seymour, and I gave up the idea of going, but General Krstic managed to find him, and he expressly ordered me that I should go to that meeting. I also remember that he had had a very serious conflict within the command with his subordinate officers regarding this order and the incident which preceded the issuing of that order. But General Krstic provided a very strong explanation, saying that the Dayton Accords should be given all the necessary support, and that I should go to that meeting. And I must say that Colonel Seymour was really very surprised, because the communications were very important; and General Krstic said that peace was all that was important, and that's why I went to the meeting. As regards the personality of General Krstic, during that period of time in my capacity as a chief engineers officer, I had very frequent contact with him, and we worked together on the implementation of those assignments very often. And he struck me both as a man and an officer. As an officer, he was always very precise and very consistent in his work. And as I said, the main focus of our work at the time was the implementation of the Dayton Accord, and he spared no effort on that work. As regards General Krstic as a man, I should like to mention the fact that General Krstic was always extremely mindful about the humanitarian side of the problems, or rather, the humane side of the problems involving this area. Very often we had to solve problems having to do with refugees, with families of the killed soldiers. Sometimes it was necessary to do some construction work for the accommodation of those people, and so on and so forth. And General Krstic always thought that it was of very high importance, that it was sometimes even more important than combat activities. I must say that I didn't know General Krstic from before -- I mean, I didn't know him very well, but that period of time made me believe that General Krstic was indeed a man and an officer of very high qualities, and that is what I wanted to say before this Honourable Chamber, because I knew General Krstic and I wanted to tell you what my view of him is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. This concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. As I have already indicated, we are now going to have a break. This would be perhaps a good moment, before we proceed with the cross-examination. Does that sound convenient to you, Mr. McCloskey, a ten-minute break at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We will have a ten-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor for the cross-examination. Please bear in mind the time that was spent for the examination-in-chief. If you forget that, I will remind you of that. And I should like also to ask you to organise your cross-examination so that public questions are asked in public session and, if necessary, we will go into private session for a limited number of questions. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Please, if you could, try to answer my questions simply. And you will always be given a chance to explain an answer, but listen to my question carefully and answer it simply, and then you can always explain, if need be. When did you and General Krstic first start working on the implementation of Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We worked together on the implementation of Dayton ever since the beginning of that process, the process of implementation of the accord, and the work became more intensive when I became chief of engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, my question was: When? And now, to help you out, Dayton occurred November 21st, 1995, just -- the anniversary was a couple of days ago. So when did you start working on the implementation of those accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, ever since that point in time, since that period of time -- and we kept receiving specific assignments, and the Dayton Accords are very specific in terms of assignments and time references. Some of the paperwork was done even before the signing of the agreement. I don't know exactly what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So there was preparations underway even before they signed the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was General Krstic present in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was present in the Drina Corps. There may have been a period of time during which he was absent for reasons of health, but he was there most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but Mr. McCloskey has asked you a very specific question: When you started working with General Krstic on the implementation of Dayton. You were told that the accords were signed on the 21st of November, 1995. You told us that you had started even before that. I have to ask you whether you started, for example, in June 1995. Tell us the exact date. It's probably a question of cultural habits. Every time a specific question is asked, you have to provide a specific answer beginning with the words contained in the actual question. So if the question is, "When did you start working together," you have to answer your question, "I started working with him on such and such date." Otherwise, we will keep wasting time. I have to ask you once again to try to do your best in answering specific questions by providing specific answers, of course. Mr. McCloskey, let us try again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't need a specific date to minutes. If you can tell us, do you know what month, perhaps, that you first started working on the implementation of what you hoped would be the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took up my duty at the time when the relevant paper was issued, and I signed it, and I joined the corps at that time with the purpose of compiling the documentation on the demining work. So that was the basis of my work on the implementation of the Dayton Accords. One of the most important things connected with that accord was exactly that, and I don't know how else I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was "what month"; what month did you start all this? Dayton was November --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I, as chief of engineers, started working as soon as I came to the corps on the 1st of February. But I told you, there had been a number of activities that we did as a battalion, in particular, the demining work around Srebrenica and Zepa, and that work was also part of the implementation of Dayton and involved drafting of the appropriate documentation. However, the real work for me started as soon as I came to the corps and took over the specific assignment and my duty in accordance with that, that is, as of the 1st of February, 1996. And ever since that time, I have been involved in this work.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, could you please switch off your microphone each time you finish your question; otherwise, we will have problems with protective measures. We don't want the witness to be heard outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I kept thinking I was about to ask a question, but I'll try to be more careful with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, it's clear that you became part of the corps in February. You also were the head of the Engineering Battalion prior to that. As the head of the Engineering Battalion prior to February, what month did you first start implementing the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the signing of the Dayton Accords, we first received the relevant documentation that had to be examined; however, specific activities concerning the implementation had begun sometime before that, and they involved the demining work of the minefields that could be removed, that is, they did not affect the security of the corps; and to the filling up of some trenches and some routes that could be filled up. So there had been a number of very specific activities which were geared to the implementation of the accords even before they were signed. But we received more detailed information only after the signing of the agreement. We received a military annex to the agreement providing for all the specific activities that we as the military had to perform. And it is very difficult for me to tell you the specific date. It was a process that took a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you sure General Krstic was present as Corps Commander from November through February, November 1995 through February 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it's very difficult for me to tell you the exact date, whether he was there or not. He was the Corps Commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and he was involved in the implementation, and he was present there. But again, (redacted) was subordinated to the Chief of Staff after that, and I received my assignments from him. So I didn't need to contact him in a direct fashion during that time, but I assumed that everything that was being done in the corps was done pursuant to the instructions of the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of the most critical parts of the Dayton Accords for the army of Republika Srpska were the presence of NATO troops on the ground in Republika Srpska; is that correct? That's a "yes" or "no" question, and if you need to explain it, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that part of the Dayton Accords included bringing NATO troops onto the ground of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew about that, and I assisted in bringing them there. I assisted Colonel Baptiste and Colonel Seymour in their arrival, and I helped them take up their positions there. I have to say that I ensured a very high level of communication with the local population. If you're referring to the 2nd Armoured Unit which was deployed along the separation line between the Drina Corps and the 2nd Corps of the BiH army, that unit was located on our side, and the command was in the immediate vicinity of our corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think this is in answer to my question, if I can interrupt the witness, but I'm -- he's just going on and on, and I would prefer to be able to try to go question by question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, as part of the preparations for the implementation of the Dayton Accords, did you receive instructions from the corps level to hide documents from the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Documents belonging to the 5th Engineering Battalion were handed over to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The answer to your question is what I have just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement to Mr. Ruez, Mr. Ruez of the ICTY, on 28 July 2000 on that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me again ask you: Did you receive instructions from the corps to do something regarding the documents of the 5th Engineering Unit because you viewed IFOR as a potential enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: See, what happened was that I handed over the documents, as I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness DE, the Prosecutor has asked you whether you received an instruction, an order, or not. The answer is "I did receive an order" or "I didn't receive an order." Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have finally understood the question. But I abide by what I have just said. However, I must add that there was a service which had a specific assignment which had to deal with the documents and which had to prevent the information from leaking. I told you about General Krstic and the implementation of Dayton Accords. This is something quite different. We had an assignment, we had a task, and we worked according to the relevant instructions. We didn't know what this new army that was coming into our area actually was. We didn't know anything about them. After all, we had been shelled by them. I'm sorry. Maybe I didn't understand you, Mr. McCloskey. I told you about my work with General Krstic, but what you asked me has to do with the Security Service, whose task was to provide adequate security in terms of intelligence and everything it entails to the unit, and that was their attitude, as you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me read to you the question and your answer and see if this helps refresh your recollection. Mr. Ruez: --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry. I see that Mr. Visnjic wishes to either make an objection or correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this time I have an objection to the document that Mr. McCloskey is about to use. The Defence believes that the situation is not the same as with our previous witness, where we had hearsay evidence. This time we have a statement given by this particular witness, and the Defence might have an opportunity later on during the direct [as interpreted] to verify the credibility of the witness. But however, in order for us to be able to do so, we would need the entire statement of the witness, and I think that, bearing this in mind, the Chamber should make an order to that effect to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe this issue has been dealt with before, but I can say it briefly. This is a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. McCloskey, but Mr. Visnjic told you about the difference. You used a document which involved some hearsay evidence. However, this time you are using a document containing the statement which was given by this witness, so the situation is different. Please bear that fact in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in fact, when Mr. Harmon did this, he used a statement not of the witness; in this particular situation, this is a statement of this actual witness. And I can tell you that the -- that what we are basing this on is the rule of law from -- that is first developed, cross-examination, in Great Britain, and it's moved over to the US. I'm a little reluctant to cite US codes since I saw someone do it in the Florida Supreme Court at his own expense, but this is a process that has been established in Britain for many years and has been adopted in the United States, and especially when it has to do with a witness; whereas using a statement like this in cross-examination, the Prosecution is allowed to use it in questioning the witness, and then if the Defence ask for it, they are allowed to view it. And if it's used to impeach the witness, then they are actually allowed to have a copy of it. And we think this is fair, it's appropriate for cross-examination, and we would hope this Court would adopt that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I ask you just one question? I'm familiar with the practice, obviously, but are you suggesting you will ask him questions on cross-examination based upon the statement, the Ruez statement that you have, then you will make that statement available to Mr. Visnjic for -- if he wants to try to rehabilitate it, if there is anything to rehabilitate, on direct? Is that what you're telling us you'll do? I want to get it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, just as it worked with Mr. Harmon before. So the appropriate part of the statement would be provided to the Defence, and so they would be allowed to use it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: By "appropriate part," you mean anything relevant to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The same thing I said to Mr. Harmon: If there was a line, two lines below that took a different point of view, they would want to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, and that's what we intend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think that's what we've been doing, hasn't it, roughly, throughout this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I thought, and that's -- the argument is the same argument and it's based again on the reciprocal discovery. We would have provided anything appropriate for the Defence under the Reciprocal Discovery Statute. It has not been asked for, not even on this particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish to add something, Mr. Visnjic? Otherwise, the Chamber will make a ruling. Do you have anything else to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have tried to find the relevant provision in the Rules that Mr. McCloskey just mentioned which refers to this particular situation, not to the situation that we had with the witness a few days ago. But I must say that I haven't found anything about this type of cross-examination in the Rules. However, if it should be the case, if I'm wrong, then I think that the Defence needs the entire statement in order to verify the credibility of the witness, if the Prosecutor insists on using the statement and if the Court allows him to do that. So in that case, we need to have an entire statement, and we hereby make this request so that we are able to conduct our redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the relevant provision of the United States law has been invoked here, but I must say that we are working on the basis of the Rules that we have. I can also invoke my domestic rules of procedure. What we have to do here is to stick to the Rules and Regulations of our Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This is what we have to use here. And our Rules provide clearly that there is no application of national law, only in case when we have to interpret our own Rules, so for the purposes of interpretation only. If you wish to test the credibility of the Defence, if anyone needs to test the credibility of the witness here, it's the Prosecution, and that is the objective of the cross-examination. They conduct their cross-examination on the basis of the examination-in-chief, and they are now conducting their cross-examination to that effect. If you have any questions arising to that, you can ask them during your additional examination on the basis of the cross-examination. The Prosecutor has to provide you relevant portions, the appropriate part that they used from the statement. But I think that in order to have -- I think that what -- that you will have enough with some enlarged portions of the appropriate text. I think that we have two basic differences here: the situation that we had some time ago when the witness was confronted with a statement of a third person, and if -- and the situation when the witness is confronted with the statement that he himself has given. We don't see how that difference in situation can entail a difference in procedure. The decision that the Chamber made for another situation will be used once again. It will be applied in this as well. That is, the Prosecutor is obliged to provide to the Defence relevant portions of the statement, in somewhat enlarged form, so that the Defence can appropriately carry out the redirect examination of the witness. Having said that, having made this ruling, or rather reapplied this ruling, I think that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And one last statement on that point: Great Britain, I believe, has since this time abandoned the rule, but it's continued in the United States, and I just wanted to make that clear. Also, Mr. Harmon reminds me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. McCloskey, our basic rule here is to have a fair and speedy trial. This is something that we have to be focussed on all the time. Please try to avoid invoking case law and statutory provisions of other countries; otherwise, I will have to speak about my domestic law as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have to add that I have profound respect for that legal system, of course. But we are applying here the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and we have to apply it; but I have, once again, profound respect for all legal procedures of the most important legal systems in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought I could get away with it on Thanksgiving, Your Honour, but I won't be getting into that any further. If I could actually now take that statement and perhaps refresh the witness' recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Mr. Ruez, what happened with the archives of the 5th Engineer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: the 5th Engineer Battalion and it was complete, everything, all the reports that were made on the level of battalion. Actually, there were some instructions from the corps level to just hide the documentation, to remove the documentation, because, you know, at the initial phases we treated SFOR as enemy forces until the situation melted out and the relationship improved. Actually, whether it was just done because of the attitude towards SFOR or some other reasons, I don't know, but that's up to the security bodies to deal with that issue, to make the assessment whether it's necessity just to move the document." And so on. So do you -- to this day, do you agree with the statement that you made to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I must say that I don't see a very big difference between what I said on the previous occasion and what I have testified about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't wish to trouble you with constant observations; however, I think that we are dealing here with a situation which we can solve once and for all. The witness does not have a statement in his own language. Mr. McCloskey is reading out to him the relevant portion of the text. As far as I understand the interpretation that I have just received, this is exactly the same as what he has stated here before the Chamber. I do not wish to discuss the interpretation; however, I think that prior to using the statement, the Prosecution should provide the statement to the witness so that the witness can have some kind of control over what he said; and also the statement should be provided to the Defence. I think that it should be useful for the future that we adopt this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, do you have a B/C/S translation of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour, and we've marked all the places that we intended to give to counsel, pursuant to the rules that have been established, and highlighted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the B/C/S version of the statement, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they don't have it yet. I think it would be convenient for the witness to have the statement in front of him. It would be preferable, at any rate, once you have the B/C/S version of the text. However, if you don't have the B/C/S version of the text, it is possible to test the credibility of the witness later on during the redirect examination if the interpretation here in court is correct. Mr. McCloskey, could you perhaps put the relevant portion of the statement before the witness, or would that be a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At this point, I don't think that violates the rule that's already been established. I hadn't planned on asking any more questions about this subject; however, I can show the witness in B/C/S what I'd read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey -- okay, okay. If you want to do that, that's fine. I will give you the opportunity to do that. You can put the B/C/S version in front of the witness, and then that will render the objection of the Defence moot; or during the additional examination, the Defence can check out whether you have correctly read out the statement or not. So for the purposes of equality of arms, I think that that should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whatever the Court prefers. I can either go on, or I can show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To speed matters up, please show this version to the witness, the portion of the text that you have just read out and on which you are basing your question. Mr. McCloskey, we should perhaps have a question and guide the witness somehow; otherwise, he will continue reading the whole text. You have to tell him which part of the text interests us here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, I have read this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that basically the way I read it, with perhaps some slight differences in translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't have the original here. Some of the things could have been translated perhaps differently, but that is more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said you were made aware of some events on the 13th of July, 1995, in the area of Konjevic Polje. Were you aware on the 16th of July that the 5th Engineering Battalion was involved in a blocking and search operation for Muslim stragglers from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that your unit was under the command of Vidoje Blagojevic on the 16th of July in those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 539/A placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could take a moment to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could push it up so we can -- actually, no, it covers the -- maybe push it up a little bit higher. Yes, thank you, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that unit mentioned in paragraph 2, the "5th INZB;" is that your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. However -- okay. Do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, the gentleman that engaged in this tour passed through Konjevic Polje, and on this communication line that he passed through, a system was established, I don't know how, but I say with full responsibility here that only in the context of that one kilometre or so stretch that I pointed out a moment ago is an area where my three guard posts were distributed which were functioning in the area. The minefields were on the flanks and outside that area, which means if he goes in order, then he went past the area of the 5th Battalion, and that -- I'm not contesting that. But the battalion never received the task -- an order about the blockade, had I seen an order or if I was shown anything like that, nor searching of the terrain. And it would be logical to suppose that when the man passed by this area, he passed the stretch that I explained earlier on because that is where it is located. And my three guard posts were there on the road, on that route; and if they were in jeopardy, then communication would be in jeopardy, too. It is also obvious, however, that you were not able to approach the area because of the minefields that blocked it off on the flanks. So you could approach it only from the Bratunac road or from the junction of at Konjevic Polje. From the direction of the village, that is. So it is an area, a stretch of about one kilometre in length.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you're not challenging the authenticity of this order regarding what was going on on July 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not in a position to challenge it or not challenge it, because this is the first time that I see it. And if the document is an authentic one, then obviously this individual did pass through Konjevic Polje, and perhaps he stopped off by the guards or the people who were there. Perhaps. I'm saying maybe. I don't know what actually he did do and whether he -- what he did in the locality or did not do. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 504/A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, this is a -- what you're reading is the handwritten notation of an intercept operator, what they heard over the airwaves on the 12th of July at 0740 hours. And the part I would like to call your attention to is the comment, "He's not. He isn't answering. Listen, please tell him that I called, that Mane, Laco's deputy, will call him, that the police in Konjevic Polje have been told to [sic] the same as the Engineering Battalion are doing, and that he can give orders to them through the commander of the Engineering Battalion." So on 12 July, who is in command at the Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know who Mane Laco's deputy might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What did you say the name was? Lacin? Laco?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just like it's written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Laco's deputy. No. No. Deputy, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that the MUP forces were in Konjevic Polje on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The MUP forces -- when I say "yes," I assume so. I wasn't there. The MUP forces had a permanent checkpoint at the Konjevic Polje junction, a permanent checkpoint. I don't know whether it was those forces or some other forces. That I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Defence Exhibit 142/B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we have it placed on the ELMO? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness' name is on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We should be in private session. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could show the witness Defence 99 and place the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, is this a document that you provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where this document came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look through the 5th Engineer archives before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to look through something else, some other kind of archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything I had I gave. I said that I took several documents later on from the company because I said that the only documents I had saved were there, as I said a moment ago. But otherwise, I did not have occasion to see any other archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear. Have you had a chance to look in some kind of military archives, aside from your own personal documents, prior to testifying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except my personal ones and a small portion of an archive which, through force of chance, was with the company commander from which I took the document I mentioned a moment ago. So certain documents, when I write an order, for example, they go to my subordinate, and that subordinate makes up his archive, and that's how it came to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who are you referring to when you say your company archive, or the archive of your company commander, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one that was on the document a moment ago in which I handed over my duty. He was the leader of that Sapper Company, and he had the Sapper Company archive as commander of that company. He received orders coming in to the company, all orders coming in or anything that he needed personally. So he had this archive of his own, and when I wanted something for myself, he would -- I wanted to get at some of the documents that were with him, and so I looked at those documents and found what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you look for the attendance roster of the 5th Engineer for that month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't keep that kind of roster, that kind of document, an attendance roster, a daily attendance roster. We didn't have that kind of document. The company commanders kept this sort of data, not the battalion command. They just saw to the command part, whereas the company leaders or commanders saw to the attendance of the men in their companies. And the principle was that there were two shifts with some companies and with others, depending on the assignment. So half the people were absent on leave, and the other have were in the unit, present in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as I understand it, the 5th Engineering Battalion kept no attendance roster?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the headquarters of the battalion, not in the unit, subordinate units. Each company for itself had an attendance roster. This was done at the -- at company level, a daily attendance roster. Not at the level of battalion, at the level of company. The company leaders, it was their duty to have this attendance, daily attendance roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you didn't look for the attendance roster that would have indicated you were not at work on these key dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to my presence and absence, that was taken care of and registered in the superior command. So I was not in a position that somebody should take care of my attendance in my own battalion. It is the superior command who sees to my attendance, and that would be the in corps command, data of that kind, with respect to me. So it is my superior officer who gives -- grants permission for leave, orders, gives me assignments, and so on, so I wouldn't -- I would be in the superior -- my attendance would have been registered by the -- in the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're still in the military, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You could have gone to the archives and looked for the documents that would have indicated that you were in Belgrade, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to look for that, but I wasn't in a position to get to that archive. When I went -- left for Belgrade, I received a piece of paper, that is to say -- but, you know, how serious papers are treated is another matter. The crossing across the River Drina, this was done with a slip of paper of smaller dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You weren't able to get to the archives; is that the answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 807.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you a little bit about the buildings in the area of the Konjevic Polje 5th Engineer Unit. I think some of these photographs you've seen before. Could you take a look at that building in this exhibit and tell me if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, but perhaps I'm wrong -- I can orientate myself better if I have a broader view. I don't want to go wrong. Could I have -- could you show me a picture taken from a different angle, from further away, because one building is very much like another, looking at it close to like this. I have -- I think I know which it is, but I'm afraid that I might go wrong, so could you give me a photograph with a wider view? But I think it is the building which was to have been the MUP command building, but as I say, I'm not quite sure. It's a similar building, but then buildings tend to be similar, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was the MUP command building located in relation to, let's say, the big school building in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That building of the MUP command, if -- you know that area where my two commands were and the communications command on that large photograph you showed me? It was moving towards the crossroads, and it was about 30 or so -- 50 metres away from me, moving towards the centre. Towards the junction, the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we show the witness Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I think we would need to hold a brief Status Conference, so perhaps this would be a good moment to interrupt our deliberations for the day because we would have to do some stocktaking with regard to next Monday, and I think there are certain aspects that the OTP would like to consider as well. So we could devote 10 minutes to that, perhaps, if you agree. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's fine. I was hoping to wrap up in about 10 or 15 minutes, but we can, we can do that tomorrow, too, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean to finish your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, let me reconsider the matter. No, but there are additional questions, questions by the Judges. No, I think it is better to stop at this point. I wanted to allow the witness to go, but I don't think that will be possible. So, Witness, we're going to meet again tomorrow at 9.20, but we have some further business to attend to here, and I should like to ask the usher to escort you out of court, but wait for the blinds to be drawn first before you leave. Witness, you will be escorted out of the courtroom, and we meet again tomorrow morning. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic, I should like to take stock of the situation as regards your witnesses. I should like to know where we are, how we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. As regards the sessions of this week, this would be the last Defence witness for this period of time. I will also give you my estimate for the following session, which, according to the schedule, should take place between the 4th and the 8th of December. During that period of time, we intend to call two additional witnesses and one military expert. So as things stand now, realistically speaking, I think that we will be able to complete during that period of time, by the 8th of December. In a special filing, we will inform the Chamber that, as regards other witnesses mentioned in our filing of the 14th of September, that we will actually forego those witnesses, that they will not be called to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. As regards the forensic expert, I will also ask the same question to the Prosecutor, but I should like to know what the situation is with your pathologist. There were two expert witnesses -- one military expert and one pathologist -- but you mentioned only this military expert. What happened with the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must say that Mr. Visnjic spent much more time with Mr. Stankovic than I did, but I will take this opportunity while I'm still on my feet to tell you that we have managed to reach an agreement with the Prosecutor as regards the written opinion of our pathologist. The Prosecutor has provided us with a written opinion of their expert, so we will be able to present the Chamber with two written reports, and we thought that it was no longer necessary for us to bring in this Defence witness to testify in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Petrusic. Is there anything else that you wish to add before I give the floor to the Prosecutor? Do you need to consult with Mr. Visnjic? No. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Harmon, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues. Your Honours, when we break, I can assure Your Honours that my colleagues and I have been working hard to try to streamline the evidence presentation in this case. We have agreed, and we have filed our notice of agreement pursuant to 94 bis (B), that we accept the opinion of -- we accept the report, I should say, as evidence of Dr. Stankovic. And in the meantime, I have provided to the Defence the reports and the comments that our experts have made in respect of Dr. Stankovic's reports. I provided my colleagues with a report of Dr. Christopher Lawrence, Dr. Wright, and today I provided them with a report of Dr. Clark. These are all their analyses and their views of the reports -- the report of Dr. Stankovic. I'm waiting for the report of Mr. Jose Baraybar so I can likewise present to my colleagues Mr. Baraybar's views of Dr. Stankovic's report. It is our hope that we will be able to present, in lieu of those witnesses testifying in our rebuttal case, their reports, and we would submit those as evidence. But my colleagues inform me that they're going to submit the reports that I have given to them to Dr. Stankovic for his views and they will let me know whether we will be in a position to merely submit the views of the experts that we have had testify in our case in chief. So in respect of Dr. Stankovic's report, we have filed our acceptance of it as a piece of evidence. Now, I have some additional issues I'd like to raise with the Court if the Court feels it's appropriate at this time. May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, we have -- this year, while we were presenting our expert testimony, we were conducting additional exhumations at additional sites that were related to this case, and in fact, Your Honour, we have conducted these exhumations at four cites: Lazete 1, Lazete 2C, Ravnice and Glogova 1. Now, this is evidence that will augment the evidence that Your Honour has heard, but because it wasn't -- because it's newly-discovered evidence in the sense that we didn't complete the exhumations until the end of the summer, we would like to present that information to Your Honours to supplement the information that we have presented previously. And with the Court's permission, I would like to file a motion, or do it orally, requesting that the Court permit us to present additional evidence in the form of reports only, summarising the findings of the experts at those various sites I've identified, and we would file with the Trial Chamber the expert reports that are related to that and the additional findings of additional ligatures, photographs, blindfolds, the number of bodies, the number of body parts. For example, at Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, those are two sites that were mentioned previously by our experts that were going to be exhumed. They were identified in the aerial image as being in close proximity to the site about which Your Honours did hear testimony. Now, I've raised this issue with my colleagues. I intend to get them and furnish the reports as soon as I receive them. I expect to receive them this month, and -- and I will get them to my colleagues, I should say, by the end of December, and I will get them to my colleagues forthwith. But I raise that because of the timetable that is facing us. We, as I understand, must present -- we have a four- or five-day block middle of January, and this application would be an application, I hope, that could be presented merely on the basis of the reports and not on -- assuming the Court granted it, would not require us to call additional evidence. Obviously, it's discretionary with the Court at this point in time, a motion that would seek to admit new evidence, but in the meantime, I raise this issue just as a possibility. I don't intend to file my motion now until I get my reports. I intend to continue my dialogue with my colleagues to see if we can reach an agreement, and then I will inform later the Trial Chamber of those developments. But I'm attempting to make sure that the Court has all the relevant evidence that it needs for its consideration, but at the same time I'm trying to be very mindful of the schedule so we don't prolong this trial inordinately. So that is one piece of information I'd like to pass on to the Trial Chamber. We have a large number of exhibits that we need to regulate. I can inform Your Honours that Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic, and I met last night in an attempt to regulate these issues. We can inform Your Honours of the conclusions that we made now or we can wait until tomorrow. I'm at your disposal. I have some additional exhibits I'd like to regulate, but I'm at your disposal as to when you want to do that, whether you want to do that today or whether you'd like to do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think tomorrow would be better, because we know more or less that the witness will complete his testimony somewhat earlier than expected, and we will have enough time to discuss all these issues. I just wanted to know whether we have to make some plans for Monday or not; that is why I wanted to know what the witness situation is. Since we will finish today [as interpreted], and early, we can discuss these matters tomorrow. Thank you very much, both of you, for notifying the Chamber about these issues. We will discuss them tomorrow, after the testimony of the witness. Thank you very much. We will adjourn for the day and come back tomorrow at 9.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
